title: The Baker's Uneven Scales (TE)
summary: A baker sues a poor farmer for selling short-weight butter. Birbal uses the baker's own loaf of bread to expose the real thief.
full_text:
In the marketplace of Agra, a baker named Karim stormed into Emperor Akbar's court, dragging a poor dairy farmer named Shambhu. The baker shouted with outrage:

'Your Majesty! This deceitful farmer has been selling me a one-pound lump of butter every morning for my pastries. This morning, I weighed his butter on my brass scales, and found it weighed only fourteen ounces instead of sixteen! He has been cheating me of two ounces of butter every day for six months! Punish this crook!'

Akbar frowned at the farmer: 'Shambhu, why do you cheat the baker? Do you have no scales?'

The poor farmer bowed with folded hands, trembling: 'Your Majesty, I am a poor man. I have no fine brass weights or scales of iron.'

'Then how do you measure the butter you sell?' Akbar demanded.

The farmer replied humbly:

'Sire, long before the baker began buying butter from me, I used to buy a one-pound loaf of bread from his bakery every morning to feed my children.

'When he asked to buy butter, I had no iron pound-weight. So every morning, when the baker sells me his one-pound loaf of bread, I place his loaf of bread on one side of my balance, and I cut a lump of butter that balances his bread on the other side!

'If my butter weighed only fourteen ounces today, it is because the loaf of bread he sold me weighed only fourteen ounces!'

The entire court fell silent!

Akbar ordered the baker's bread brought from his cart immediately. Birbal placed the loaf upon the royal mint scale in the center of the hall.

The needle swung: exactly fourteen ounces! The baker had been cheating his customers by selling underweight bread, and the farmer had merely balanced the butter against the baker's own short-weight loaf!

The baker turned red as a beet and dropped to his knees, begging for mercy.

Birbal smiled with razor-sharp justice:

'The ancient proverb is fulfilled, Karim: "With what measure you mete, it shall be measured to you again." You cheated the poor with light bread, and nature returned the exact same weight to your own doorstep!'

Akbar fined the dishonest baker one hundred gold coins to be given to the farmer, and ordered the baker's shop monitored by the city magistrates.
